**Video:** [Tutorial 15 Part 1 — RNNs, LSTMs and GRUs](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zM5-TlrmKg8)

## Learning goals

- Write the basic RNN recurrence and see weight sharing across time.
- Explain vanishing/exploding gradients as the motive for gated units.
- Contrast LSTM and GRU at the level of **cell state** and **gates**.

## Before this clicks

A sequence $x_1,\ldots,x_T$ (tokens, frames, sensor readings) has order that matters. An RNN keeps a hidden state $h_t$ that summarizes “what happened so far,” updated with the **same** weights at every $t$. Training unrolls the graph in time (**BPTT**). Long unrollings multiply many Jacobians $\Rightarrow$ gradients can shrink or blow up; LSTMs/GRUs add gates so memory can pass more stably.

---

## Main ideas

### 1. Vanilla RNN

$$
h_t=\tanh(W_{xh}x_t+W_{hh}h_{t-1}+b),\qquad
\hat{y}_t=\mathrm{softmax}(W_{hy}h_t+c)
$$

(or a single label from $h_T$). Parameters $(W_{xh},W_{hh},\ldots)$ do not depend on $t$.

### 2. Batching sequences

Minibatches pad/pack variable lengths. A batch tensor is often `(batch, time, features)`. Masks ignore pad steps in the loss. Teacher forcing (for generation) feeds the true previous token during training.

### 3. Why gates?

In a deep-in-time tanh RNN, $\partial h_T/\partial h_1$ is a product of many factors with singular values often $<1$ $\Rightarrow$ **vanishing** gradients; $>1$ $\Rightarrow$ **exploding** (clipping helps explosions; architecture helps vanishing).

### 4. LSTM (intuition)

Maintain a **cell** $c_t$ as a highway for long-range memory, plus gates in $(0,1)$:

- **Forget** $f_t$: how much of $c_{t-1}$ to keep.
- **Input** $i_t$: how much new candidate $\tilde{c}_t$ to write.
- **Output** $o_t$: how much of $c_t$ to expose as $h_t$.

Schematically:

$$
c_t=f_t\odot c_{t-1}+i_t\odot\tilde{c}_t,\qquad
h_t=o_t\odot\tanh(c_t).
$$

### 5. GRU (intuition)

Fewer tensors than LSTM: a **reset** gate and an **update** gate blend previous hidden state with a candidate — no separate cell. Often similar accuracy, cheaper.

| Model | Memory path | Gate count (rough) |
|-------|-------------|--------------------|
| RNN | $h_t$ only | none |
| LSTM | $c_t$ + $h_t$ | forget, input, output |
| GRU | $h_t$ with update/reset | two |

---

## Worked mini-example

Binary sequence: predict next bit. Tiny RNN with $h\in\mathbb{R}^{2}$. After seeing `1,0,1`, $h_3$ should differ from $h_3$ after `0,0,0` if the recurrence mixes past inputs. For a long run of identical bits, a vanilla RNN’s $\partial L/\partial W_{hh}$ may nearly vanish; an LSTM can keep $f_t\approx 1$ so $c_t$ carries the early “I saw a 1” signal forward with less attenuation.

---

## Common confusions

| Confusion | Clarification |
|-----------|---------------|
| RNN = only language | Any ordered sequence; audio, video, time series too |
| LSTM “solves” all long memory | Helps a lot; still finite capacity; attention/transformers go further |
| GRU outdated vs LSTM | Often competitive; pick by validation |
| Batch time axis is optional | Need a clear time (or pack) dimension for recurrence |
